title: What is the difference between aligned checkpoints (all channels must receive barrier before snapshot, can cause backpressure amplification) and unaligned checkpoints (Flink 1.11+, snapshot includes in-flight data, reduces checkpoint duration under backpressure)?
shortTitle: Aligned vs unaligned checkpoints in Flink

s1_definition.profdef: Aligned and unaligned checkpoints are two modes for how a multi-input operator snapshots during Flink's barrier-based checkpointing. In an aligned checkpoint, an operator that receives a barrier on one input channel waits, buffering that channel, until the barrier has arrived on all input channels before it snapshots, which keeps the snapshot free of in-flight data but can amplify backpressure because fast channels stall waiting for slow ones. In an unaligned checkpoint, introduced in Flink 1.11, the operator snapshots immediately when the first barrier arrives and includes the in-flight records sitting in its input and output buffers as part of the snapshot, so the barrier can overtake buffered records, which dramatically shortens checkpoint duration under backpressure at the cost of larger snapshots.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants a consistent photo of its processing line. In the aligned approach, a clerk fed by two conveyors who sees the colored barrier slip on one conveyor must freeze that conveyor and wait until the colored slip also appears on the other conveyor before taking the photo. If one conveyor is slow, the clerk waits a long time and the fast conveyor backs up, holding up the whole line. In the unaligned approach, the moment the clerk sees the colored slip on any conveyor, they immediately photograph not only their passbook but also every slip currently sitting in their in-trays and out-trays, and let the colored slip jump ahead. The photo is bigger because it includes those in-flight slips, but it is taken right away so nothing stalls.
s1_definition.oneliner: Aligned checkpoints wait for all barriers and exclude in-flight data but stall under backpressure, while unaligned checkpoints snapshot immediately including in-flight data to stay fast under backpressure.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Aligned and unaligned checkpoints are two modes for how a multi-input operator snapshots during Flink's barrier-based checkpointing. In an aligned checkpoint, an operator that receives a barrier on one input channel waits, buffering that channel, until the barrier has arrived on all input channels before it snapshots, which keeps the snapshot free of in-flight data but can amplify backpressure because fast channels stall waiting for slow ones. In an unaligned checkpoint, introduced in Flink 1.11, the operator snapshots immediately when the first barrier arrives and includes the in-flight records sitting in its input and output buffers as part of the snapshot, so the barrier can overtake buffered records, which dramatically shortens checkpoint duration under backpressure at the cost of larger snapshots.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants a consistent photo of its processing line. In the aligned approach, a clerk fed by two conveyors who sees the colored barrier slip on one conveyor must freeze that conveyor and wait until the colored slip also appears on the other conveyor before taking the photo. If one conveyor is slow, the clerk waits a long time and the fast conveyor backs up, holding up the whole line. In the unaligned approach, the moment the clerk sees the colored slip on any conveyor, they immediately photograph not only their passbook but also every slip currently sitting in their in-trays and out-trays, and let the colored slip jump ahead. The photo is bigger because it includes those in-flight slips, but it is taken right away so nothing stalls.

**One line to remember:** Aligned checkpoints wait for all barriers and exclude in-flight data but stall under backpressure, while unaligned checkpoints snapshot immediately including in-flight data to stay fast under backpressure.

sections.s2_technical:
In aligned checkpointing, when a barrier for checkpoint N arrives on one input channel of a multi-input operator, the operator performs alignment: it stops consuming that channel and buffers any further records from it, while continuing to process the other channels until their barriers for checkpoint N also arrive. Once all channels have delivered the barrier, the operator snapshots its state, which at that moment reflects exactly all pre-barrier records and no post-barrier records, and then forwards the barrier and drains the buffered records. The strength is a clean, minimal snapshot with no in-flight records to store. The weakness is that if one input channel is slow, perhaps because of skew or a slow upstream, the operator waits for its barrier while buffering the fast channels, and that waiting propagates backpressure upstream and can make the checkpoint take a very long time or even time out. Under heavy backpressure, aligned checkpoints can effectively fail to complete.

In unaligned checkpointing, the operator does not wait for all barriers. As soon as the first barrier for checkpoint N arrives on any input channel, Flink immediately takes the snapshot and crucially includes the in-flight data: the records already buffered in the operator's input and output network buffers become part of the checkpoint. The barrier is then allowed to overtake those buffered records and race downstream. Because the operator snapshots at once rather than waiting for the slowest channel, the checkpoint completes quickly even under severe backpressure, which keeps checkpoints reliable exactly when the system is stressed. The cost is that the snapshot is larger, since it must persist the in-flight buffer contents, and recovery must replay those in-flight records, so checkpoint storage and restore are heavier.

How you choose: aligned is the traditional default and is fine when the job is not backpressured, producing small, clean snapshots. You enable unaligned checkpoints, often with an alignment timeout so Flink starts aligned and automatically switches to unaligned only if alignment takes too long, when your job experiences backpressure and aligned checkpoints are timing out or taking too long. The senior nuances are that unaligned checkpoints trade larger state and heavier recovery for reliable, fast checkpointing under load; that they are primarily beneficial for jobs with backpressure and exactly-once requirements; that they do not help much for jobs that are not backpressured; and that the alignment-timeout hybrid is often the best practical setting, because it keeps snapshots small in normal operation and only pays the unaligned cost when the system is actually struggling. Unaligned checkpoints also require exactly-once mode and have some restrictions, such as not combining with certain features, which you must check for your version.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a stateful enrichment job that joins the live transaction stream with a slower reference stream. During market-open spikes, the transaction input floods in while the reference input lags, so a multi-input operator receiving the barrier on the fast transaction channel must wait for the barrier on the slow reference channel. With aligned checkpoints, this waiting buffers the flood of fast-channel records and amplifies backpressure, and checkpoints start taking far too long and risk timing out. This is exactly the aligned-checkpoint backpressure-amplification problem.

Problem 2 — To keep checkpoints completing reliably during those spikes, the bank switches the operator to unaligned checkpoints, so it snapshots immediately on the first barrier and captures the in-flight records in its buffers rather than waiting for the slow channel. Checkpoints now complete quickly even under backpressure, at the cost of a larger snapshot. This is exactly the unaligned-checkpoint benefit and tradeoff.

In the mini-project we build a runnable demo that contrasts the two modes on a two-input operator with one fast and one slow channel. We define a `Signal` that is a record or a barrier. A `CheckpointableOperator` has a mode flag. In aligned mode it waits for barriers on both channels, buffering the fast channel, and reports the simulated wait as the number of buffered records. In unaligned mode it snapshots on the first barrier, captures the in-flight buffered records into the snapshot, and reports near-zero wait with a larger snapshot size. An `AlignedVsUnalignedDemo` main class feeds a fast channel that barriers early and keeps sending, and a slow channel that barriers late, then runs the same scenario in both modes and prints the wait time and snapshot size so the tradeoff is visible.

Configuration file:

```yaml
# application.yml
flink:
  checkpoint:
    unaligned: true                 # enable unaligned checkpoints
    aligned-timeout-ms: 5000        # start aligned, switch to unaligned after this
    mode: EXACTLY_ONCE
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a two-input operator fed by a fast transaction channel and a slow reference channel, under backpressure, processed once in aligned mode and once in unaligned mode.

Step 1, Aligned mode: The fast transaction channel sends a record and then its barrier. The operator notes that the transaction channel has barriered, one of two inputs, but the reference channel has not, so it cannot snapshot yet.

Step 2, Aligned continues: The fast channel keeps flooding five more records while the reference barrier is delayed. Because the transaction channel has already barriered and the reference channel has not, the operator must buffer all five of these fast-channel records, which represents the alignment wait and the backpressure building up.

Step 3, Aligned finishes: The slow reference channel finally sends a record and its barrier. Now both inputs are barriered, so the operator snapshots, but it had to wait and buffer five records to get here. The reported alignment-buffered count is five, representing the backpressure amplification caused by waiting on the slow channel.

Step 4, Unaligned mode: The fast transaction channel sends a record and then its barrier. In unaligned mode the operator does not wait; it snapshots immediately on this first barrier and captures the in-flight buffered records at that moment into the snapshot.

Step 5, Unaligned continues: The fast channel sends five more records, but the operator has already snapshotted for this checkpoint, so it does not need to buffer them for alignment. The checkpoint is already done; the barrier has effectively overtaken the in-flight data.

Step 6, Unaligned finishes: The slow reference channel sends its record and barrier, but the snapshot was already taken long before, so there is zero alignment wait. The reported in-flight captured count reflects the records that were in the buffer when the snapshot fired, which makes the snapshot larger, but the checkpoint completed immediately. The contrast is clear: aligned waited and amplified backpressure, unaligned completed instantly with a bigger snapshot.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] === ALIGNED mode (under backpressure) ===
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] ALIGNED snapshot after both barriers; waited on 5 buffered fast-channel records
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] ALIGNED snapshotted=true alignmentBuffered=5 inFlightCaptured=0
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] === UNALIGNED mode (under backpressure) ===
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] UNALIGNED snapshot on first barrier from txn capturing 1 in-flight records
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] UNALIGNED snapshotted=true alignmentBuffered=0 inFlightCaptured=1
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Aligned and unaligned checkpoints are two modes for how a multi-input operator takes its snapshot during Flink's barrier-based checkpointing, and the difference matters most under backpressure. In an aligned checkpoint, when the barrier for a checkpoint arrives on one input channel, the operator stops consuming that channel and buffers its further records while it waits for the barrier to arrive on all the other input channels. Only when every channel has delivered the barrier does it snapshot, which gives a clean, minimal snapshot containing exactly the pre-barrier records and nothing in flight. The weakness is that if one input channel is slow, the operator sits there waiting while buffering the fast channels, and that waiting propagates backpressure upstream, so under heavy load aligned checkpoints can take very long or time out entirely, which is dangerous because that is exactly when you most want reliable checkpoints.

Unaligned checkpoints, added in Flink 1.11, fix this. Instead of waiting for all barriers, the operator snapshots immediately when the first barrier arrives on any channel, and it includes the in-flight records sitting in its input and output network buffers as part of the snapshot. The barrier is then allowed to overtake those buffered records and race downstream. Because the snapshot happens at once rather than waiting for the slowest channel, the checkpoint completes quickly even under severe backpressure. The tradeoff is that the snapshot is larger, since it must persist the in-flight buffer contents, and recovery is heavier because those in-flight records must be replayed. The practical sweet spot is a hybrid: enable unaligned checkpoints with an alignment timeout, so the job starts each checkpoint aligned and keeps snapshots small during normal operation, but automatically switches to unaligned only when alignment takes too long, paying the larger-snapshot cost only when the system is genuinely struggling.

At the National Bank of India this came up in an enrichment job that joined the fast live transaction stream with a slower reference stream. During market-open spikes, the transaction input flooded in while the reference input lagged, and with aligned checkpoints the operator buffered the transaction flood while waiting for the reference barrier, amplifying backpressure until checkpoints started timing out. We enabled unaligned checkpoints with an alignment timeout of a few seconds, so that in calm periods we still got small aligned snapshots, but during spikes the operator snapshotted immediately, captured the in-flight buffers, and kept checkpoints completing reliably. I could demonstrate the contrast concretely: aligned mode had to buffer a run of fast-channel records and waited on the slow channel, while unaligned mode snapshotted on the first barrier with zero wait at the cost of a bigger snapshot. Being able to explain the backpressure-amplification problem of alignment, the in-flight-data mechanism of unaligned checkpoints, and the alignment-timeout hybrid as the real-world default is exactly the depth an interviewer is looking for.
